Affinity

uh-FIN-ih-tee — think of 'affinity' as a fine connection you feel toward something. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Affinity is a natural liking or attraction toward something.

He discovered an unexpected affinity for pottery the very first time he touched a spinning wheel.

Worked Example

A child who has never had a formal lesson sits down at a piano and immediately starts picking out simple tunes by ear, grinning the entire time and asking to play again the next day.

A natural, easy pull toward something — without being taught to feel it — is an affinity. Unlike 'talent,' which describes skill, affinity describes the pull of genuine liking itself.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

fondness: a warm liking for something

attraction: a pull or draw toward something

inclination: a natural tendency or preference

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

aversion: a strong dislike or unwillingness

distaste: a dislike for something

Where it sits · how strong the pull toward it is — interest → affinity → passion

interest vs. affinity: Interest is weaker than affinity — you can be interested in something without feeling truly drawn to it, while affinity is a genuine natural pull.

passion vs. affinity: Passion is stronger than affinity: affinity is a natural liking, but passion is an intense, driving devotion that goes far beyond simple liking.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — af- (ad-)

prefix — af- (ad-): to, toward (Latin)

root — -fin-

root — -fin-: border, end (Latin)

suffix — -ity

suffix — -ity: state or quality of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin affinitas literally meant 'bordering on' — ad- (toward) plus finis (border, end). An affinity was originally a close connection, a shared border, and came to mean a natural pull or closeness toward something.

Use the root in a new word: finite

Use the root in a new word: finite: Even the universe may have a finite number of stars, though we can't count them all.
